chapters.title: Chapter 1: Characteristics and Life Process of Organisms

lessons.title: Characteristics of Living Things
lessons.notes_html:
What Makes a Thing Living?

Living things are different from non-living things because they show special characteristics. The main characteristics of living things are:

  • They breathe.
  • They use food to remain alive and to get energy.
  • They reproduce offspring of their own kind.
  • They can move on their own.
  • They can grow.
  • They can sense changes around them.

Living things also show excretion and sensitivity. Both plants and animals are living things, and both need food, sunlight, water and air.

Key Facts

  • The characteristic common among a butterfly, a bird and a bat is that they all have wings.
  • Plants provide oxygen to the environment.

lessons.title: Plants and Animals: Similarities and Differences
lessons.notes_html:
Two Major Groups of Living Things

The two major groups of living things are plants and animals. Mango trees and goats are both living things, but they differ from each other in many ways.

Similarities between Plants and Animals

  • Both grow.
  • Both respire (breathe).
  • Both reproduce.
  • Both need food, sunlight, water and air.

Differences between Plants and Animals

PlantsAnimals
Usually green in colourUsually of various colours
Prepare their own foodDepend on plants and other animals for their food
Cannot move from one place to anotherCan move from one place to another

Plants have roots, stems and leaves, while animals have sense organs and organs for movement.

lessons.title: Vertebrates and Invertebrates
lessons.notes_html:
Classification of Animals

Animals are divided into two major groups on the basis of whether they have a backbone or not. The line of bones you can feel at the back of your neck is called the backbone or vertebral column.

Vertebrates

Vertebrates are the animals having a backbone. Examples are fish, frog, lizard, pigeon, cat and human beings. The statement that is correct for all vertebrates is: they have a backbone.

Invertebrates

Invertebrates are the animals having no backbone. Examples are honey bee, cockroach, butterfly, starfish, snail, insects and worms. A butterfly is an example of an invertebrate.

How Invertebrates Are Useful for Humans

  • Bees pollinate flowers and give us honey.
  • Earthworms make the soil fertile.
  • Silkworms give us silk.
  • Many invertebrates are food for other animals.

lessons.title: Flowering and Non-Flowering Plants
lessons.notes_html:
Classification of Plants

Plants are divided into two major groups: flowering plants and non-flowering plants.

Flowering Plants

Plants on which flowers grow are called flowering plants. Mustard, sunflower, rose, guava, lemon and apple are examples of flowering plants. Flowering plants may be herbs, shrubs and trees, and they are of various colours and sizes.

  • Many plants produce fruits to protect their seeds.
  • The part of a plant that is absent in non-flowering plants is the fruit.
  • A flower is the reproductive part of a plant. It produces seeds and fruits, attracts insects for pollination, and adds beauty and fragrance to nature.

Non-Flowering Plants

The plants on which flowers do not grow are called non-flowering plants. Moss, fern and conifers (for example pine, juniper, thuja and sago palm) are examples of non-flowering plants. The pine is a non-flowering plant.

Interesting Information: Conifers

Conifers are found in the northern areas of Pakistan in places like Murree, Swat, Kaghan and Chilas. Their wood is used for making furniture, construction materials and ornamental things, and also to make paper. The seeds of some conifers are used as dry fruit, such as pine nut (chilghoza).

lessons.title: Biodiversity
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Biodiversity?

The various types of living things found at a particular place are called biodiversity. We still do not know the actual number and kinds of living things present on the Earth.

Importance of Biodiversity

Biodiversity keeps the ecosystem balanced. Different kinds of plants and animals provide food, clean air, medicines and raw materials, and every kind has a role in nature.

Biodiversity in Danger

  • Some living things have become extinct.
  • The existence of many living things is in danger due to destruction of habitat, change of climate and scarcity of water over years.
  • The Government of Pakistan has started plantation of billions of trees to stop climate change.
  • Located near Lahore, Changa Manga is the largest man-made forest in the world.

lessons.title: Teeth, Bones and Muscles
lessons.notes_html:
Teeth and Their Functions

Digestion essentially starts by chewing. Teeth help in breaking down the food into smaller pieces. There are four types of teeth, and each type performs its own function:

NameFunction
IncisorsBiting and cutting food
CaninesPiercing and tearing food
PremolarsChewing and grinding food
MolarsChewing and grinding food
  • A tiger has large canines. It uses its large, sharp canines to catch its prey and to tear the flesh of the animals it eats.
  • A rat has large incisors. It uses them to gnaw and cut hard food and other materials into small pieces.

Bones

Most of the bones in the human body are hard, and they are of various sizes and shapes. All the bones of the body make a frame called the skeleton. There are 206 bones in the human skeleton. The places where two or more bones meet are called joints. The bones of the arm and leg are hollow; they have bone marrow, which helps to produce blood.

Muscles

The muscles of the human body are attached to the bones. They are soft and pink or red in colour. There are almost 600 muscles in a human body, and almost half of the body weight is due to muscles. When we smile, 14 muscles are needed.

How Bones and Muscles Work Together

Bones and muscles work together to produce movement. When the muscles contract, they pull the various parts of our bones, and the bone moves at the joint. Muscles work in pairs: when one muscle contracts, the other relaxes. Due to these movements we can sit, walk, run and jump. Muscles also help the heart to pump blood and move food through the digestive system.

lessons.title: Lungs, Heart, Stomach and Brain
lessons.notes_html:
Lungs

During breathing, air enters our lungs through the nose. From the nose, air goes into a windpipe, which opens into the two lungs. The lungs are surrounded by ribs. They keep on expanding and contracting, and the exchange of oxygen between blood and air takes place in the lungs. In short, the lungs take in oxygen from the air and remove carbon dioxide from the body during breathing.

Heart

The heart is located on the upper left side of the chest, surrounded by the ribs. It works continuously like a pump throughout life. The muscles of the heart contract and relax, and this keeps on circulating blood all over the body through blood vessels. The heart pumps blood to all parts of the body, carrying oxygen and food to the cells.

Stomach

The stomach is a bag-like organ. It is located on the left side of our body below the heart, and it is the biggest part of the digestive tract. It secretes digestive juice. The muscles of the stomach move and grind the food, and the digestive juice breaks down (digests) the food.

Brain

The brain is the most important part of our body. It is located within our skull. It controls all the functions of our body. It collects information from different parts of our body and decides the type of response our body should give.

Project Activity: Simulating the Heart's Pumping of Blood

Stretch a cut balloon over the mouth of a jar half-filled with coloured water. Fit two straws through holes in the balloon and seal one straw tip. Press the balloon again and again: the coloured water comes out of the open straw, just as the heart pumps blood through the body.

lessons.title: Parts of a Plant and Their Functions
lessons.notes_html:
Five Important Parts of a Flowering Plant

The five important parts of a flowering plant are root, stem, leaf, flower and seed. Each of these parts performs its particular function.

Root

The root is present under the ground. Its branches spread in different directions. The roots anchor the plant in the soil and absorb water and minerals from it.

Stem

The stem grows above the ground. It has many branches, and there are many leaves on the stem and its branches. The stem transports water and minerals from the root to the leaves. It also supports the plant.

Leaf

Leaves are of different sizes and shapes, and usually their colour is green. One of the most important functions of the leaf is to make food for the plant. The parts of a leaf are: lamina (the flat part), midrib, vein and petiole (the stalk).

Flower, Fruit and Seeds

Flowering plants have beautiful flowers of different sizes and colours. Fruits and seeds are formed from the flowers. When seeds are formed within the flower, the area surrounding the seed ripens into fruit. Some fruits, such as mango, apricot and peach, have only one seed. Some fruits have many seeds, such as watermelon, papaya and guava. When a seed is sown, a new plant grows (germinates) from it.

lessons.title: Environment and Ecosystem
lessons.notes_html:
Environment

The environment is everything that surrounds a living thing, including all living and non-living things around it, such as air, water, soil, plants and animals.

Ecosystem

An ecosystem is the collection of abiotic and biotic components in an area — a system of living things interacting with their environment.

Conservation of the Ecosystem

For the conservation of the ecosystem, tree plantation is being done. Cutting forests, building roads and installing factories do not conserve the ecosystem.

lessons.title: Biotic and Abiotic Components
lessons.notes_html:
Biotic Components

All the biotic components are living things. The three biotic components of an ecosystem are:

  • Producers — green plants, which make their own food.
  • Consumers — animals, which eat other living things.
  • Decomposers — bacteria and fungi, which break down dead things.

Abiotic Components

Three abiotic (non-living) components of an ecosystem are air, water and soil. Light and temperature are also abiotic components.

lessons.title: Food Chains and a Balanced Ecosystem
lessons.notes_html:
Food Chain

A food chain begins with a producer. A simple food chain is:

Grass (producer) → Grasshopper (consumer) → Frog (consumer) → Snake (consumer) → Hawk (consumer)

Energy passes from one living thing to the next in this order.

Predator and Prey

If the food resources increase, the population of prey animals grows, so predators get more food and their population also increases.

Biodiversity and Competition

In a balanced ecosystem, many kinds of living things share food, water and space, so they compete with one another. This competition keeps every population in check, and biodiversity keeps the ecosystem stable and healthy.

Investigate: Ostriches

  • The female ostrich is grey-brown in colour, so during the day she blends with the sandy ground and enemies cannot easily see her while she sits on the eggs.
  • The male ostrich is black in colour, so at night he blends with the darkness and enemies cannot easily see him while he sits on the eggs.

lessons.title: Human Actions and Saving the Ecosystem
lessons.notes_html:
Human Activities Affecting the Ecosystem

Two human activities affecting the ecosystem are cutting down forests (deforestation) and polluting air, water and land with smoke, chemicals and waste.

Effect of Insecticides

If insecticides are used for controlling the population of insects, the population of birds will decrease, because the birds lose their food and are also poisoned through the food chain.

Project Activity: Make an Ecosystem Model

Cut two bottles. Pour water in one to show an aquatic ecosystem, and put soil and a small plant in the other to show a land ecosystem. Connect the two with a thick thread so the plant receives water and minerals. Observe daily and write a report.

lessons.title: Illness and Diseases
lessons.notes_html:
Reasons of Illness

Three reasons of illness are: germs entering the body, eating an unbalanced diet, and living in dirty surroundings or drinking dirty water.

Fever

The normal body temperature is 98.6 degrees F. If our body temperature increases from 98.6 degrees F to 101 degrees F, its cause is fever.

How Coughing Benefits the Body

Coughing clears dust, germs and mucus out of the air passages, so the lungs stay clean and breathing becomes easier.

Contagious and Non-Contagious Diseases

  • Contagious diseases spread from one person to another through germs, such as flu and measles.
  • Non-contagious diseases do not spread from person to person, such as diabetes and heart disease.

Polio is caused by a virus.

lessons.title: Prevention of Contagious Diseases
lessons.notes_html:
Protection against Contagious Diseases

Protection against contagious diseases is mainly done by wearing a mask, washing hands and vaccination.

  • If you have flu, you should wear a mask to keep others safe from infection.
  • Washing hands properly is an important habit. The book shows seven steps for hand washing.

How Vaccination Protects Us

Vaccination trains the body's defence system to recognise and fight particular germs, so when the real germs enter the body, it can destroy them before we fall ill.

lessons.title: Balanced Diet and Good Health
lessons.notes_html:
Balanced Diet

A balanced diet is a diet in which all the components of food — carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water — are present in proper amounts.

Food Groups

Foods are divided into groups. The fruit and vegetable group includes fruits such as apple, orange and banana, and different vegetables. Among meat, rice, milk and pulses, milk has the highest amount of calcium.

Activities

  • Investigate: interview a doctor or a health worker and ask about the principles of living a healthy life. Write their responses in the table given in the book.
  • Project: observe the kitchen of your home, find out the factors which may cause diseases, and write each factor with its way of prevention in the table given in the book.

lessons.title: Clean Drinking Water
lessons.notes_html:
Drinking Water Filtration Plant

Function of a Filter

A filter removes dirt and solid impurities from water, so the water becomes clean and clear for drinking.

Does Filtration Remove Germs?

Filtration removes dirt but it does not remove all the germs from water, so filtered water still needs further treatment to be fully safe.

Killing Germs in Water

Germs in water can be killed by boiling the water or by adding chlorine to it.

Making Water Safe for Drinking

Water can be made safe for drinking by filtering it to remove dirt, then boiling it or chlorinating it to kill germs, and keeping it covered in a clean container.

lessons.title: Matter and Its States
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Matter?

Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.

Three States of Matter

Matter exists in three states: solid, liquid and gas. Snow, cloud and steam are an example of the three states of matter together: snow is a solid, the tiny water drops in a cloud are liquid, and steam is a gas.

Properties of Solids and Liquids

  • Solids have a definite shape and a definite volume. They do not become smaller on pressing.
  • Liquids have a definite volume but no definite shape. When a liquid is poured into any vessel, it gets the shape of that vessel.

lessons.title: Mass and Volume
lessons.notes_html:
Mass

The amount of matter in an object is called its mass.

  • The mass of a matter never changes in any condition.
  • Mass is measured in grams or kilograms. 1 kilogram = 1000 grams.

Volume

The space that an object occupies is called its volume. Among a book, a pencil, a scale and a cricket bat, the cricket bat has the most volume, because it occupies the most space.

lessons.title: Arrangement of Particles in Solids, Liquids and Gases
lessons.notes_html:
Particles of Matter

All matter consists of very tiny particles. The arrangement of particles in solid, liquid and gas is different.

StateArrangement of ParticlesShape and Volume
SolidParticles are strongly attached and closely packed in fixed positions; they only vibrate and do not change their positionDefinite shape and definite volume
LiquidParticles are close to one another but the force of attraction is weaker; they keep colliding and can move near or far from one anotherDefinite volume but no definite shape
GasParticles are far apartNo definite shape and no definite volume

Differences between Solids and Liquids

Solids have a fixed shape and a fixed volume, while liquids have a fixed volume but no fixed shape — they take the shape of their container. The particles of solids are closely packed, while the particles of liquids are less tightly packed and can move.

Density of the States

Gas has the lowest density, because its particles are far apart and it has very little mass in a given volume.

lessons.title: Floating, Sinking and Density
lessons.notes_html:
Density

Two objects having equal volume may have different masses. The floating and sinking of objects depends on their density — the mass present in a definite volume.

  • Objects having less density than water float on water.
  • Objects having more density than water sink in it.

Ice in Water

A piece of ice put into a glass of water floats at the surface of the water, because ice is less dense than water.

Coldest to Hottest

Water, ice and steam all have different temperatures. Their order from coldest to hottest is: ice, water, steam.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Metals
lessons.notes_html:
Metals Are Good Conductors of Heat

If two spoons made of steel and wood are put in a cup of hot water, after a few minutes the steel spoon becomes hot whereas the wooden spoon does not. This shows that metal is a better conductor of heat than wood.

  • Cooking utensils are made of metals because metals are good conductors of heat, so food cooks quickly, and metals are strong and do not break easily.
  • Metals such as copper, aluminium and silver allow electricity to pass through them, so they are used to make electric wires.

Colours of Metals

Metals have various colours. Gold is yellow, copper is red, silver is white, tin and nickel are light pink, and zinc, chromium and aluminium are light blue in colour. Most of the metals are grey in colour. Some metals have magnetic properties and are attracted by a magnet.

Why Metal Is Used in a Bell

Metal is used in making a bell because when metal is struck it vibrates and produces a clear, loud sound that carries far.

Why Metals Are Preferred for Ornaments

Metals are preferred for ornaments because they are shiny, they can be shaped easily, and they do not rust or spoil quickly.

Insulators Keep Us Safe

Electricians wear rubber gloves while repairing an electric switchboard because rubber is an insulator of electricity. The gloves stop electric current from passing into their bodies, so they stay safe from electric shock.

A Table Can Tell Us about Matter

Matter No. 1, which transmits heat quickly, is a solid and does not dissolve in water, is iron. Matter No. 2, which transmits heat slowly, is a solid and dissolves in water, is sugar.

Project Activity

Collect five things made of metals, observe them, and write their metal, appearance, texture and colour in the table given in the book.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Forms of Energy and Energy Transfer

lessons.title: Energy and Its Sources
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Energy?

Energy is the ability to do work. Human beings and animals use energy for their movements. We observe energy as light in lamps, as heat in heaters, and as sound in doorbells.

Sources of Energy

We get energy from many sources. Among the sources of energy are the Sun, fast-flowing water, air (wind), coal, oil, gas and wood. Plants get energy for growth from the Sun.

Forms of Energy

Light, sound and heat are forms of energy. Glass is not a form of energy, and neither is plastic.

lessons.title: Conservation of Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Limited Resources

Sources of energy like coal, oil and gas are limited resources on Earth. We are unable to increase their amounts, because they were made in millions of years.

Saving Energy

We can save these resources by consuming them carefully. As our population increases, we should keep a balance between the facilities we need for a comfortable life and the limited sources of energy, so that not only we but also the next generations do not face energy shortage.

lessons.title: Light: How It Travels and Forms Shadows
lessons.notes_html:
Light

Light is a form of energy that helps us to see the things around us. The Sun, stars and lightning are natural sources of light. Candle, oil lamp, torchlight and electric bulb are artificial sources of light.

How Light Travels

  • When light leaves its source, it travels in all directions in straight lines, and it can pass through some objects.
  • Light can travel through vacuum. Heat can also travel through vacuum by radiation, but sound cannot travel through vacuum.

Shadows

When your hand comes between a lamp and a wall, a shadow of the hand forms on the wall. The shadow is larger when the hand is nearer to the lamp, and smaller when the hand moves away from it.

lessons.title: Reflection of Light and the Rainbow
lessons.notes_html:
Reflection of Light

In the morning, you usually see your image in the mirror. When light strikes the shiny and smooth surface of a mirror, it bounces back and enters our eye. In this way, we can see our image in the mirror. This is called the reflection of light.

Seven Colours of Sunlight

A prism is a three-faced transparent object which divides light into different colours. There are seven colours in sunlight.

The Rainbow

We can see a rainbow when it rains and the Sun shines at the same time. Sunlight splits into seven colours as it passes through the raindrops, and this band of colours is the rainbow.

lessons.title: Sound Energy and Echo
lessons.notes_html:
Sound Energy

Sound is the form of energy that is produced by vibration in an object. These vibrations reach our ears through the particles of the air. In this way, we hear sounds. When we speak, our vocal cords in the throat vibrate and produce sounds.

Sound Needs a Medium

  • Sound needs some medium to travel. Most of the sounds reach us by travelling through air.
  • Sound cannot travel in space (vacuum). This is why we cannot hear the sounds of the explosions in the Sun.
  • Astronauts talk with each other using radio waves, because radio waves can travel through vacuum, unlike sound.

Echo

Sound is also reflected, similar to light. When sound bounces back from an object (a wall) at a certain distance and we hear it again, it is called an echo. Bats use echoes to catch their prey in darkness: they emit sounds from their mouth and, by sensing the echoes, they find their way in darkness.

Sensing the Buzzing of a Mosquito

The mosquito's wings vibrate and produce sound waves that travel through the air to our ears, and our ears sense these vibrations as a buzzing sound.

lessons.title: Heat and Temperature
lessons.notes_html:
Heat

Heat is a form of energy that always travels from a hot object to a cold object.

Temperature and the Thermometer

We use the term temperature to measure the hotness or coldness of an object. The instrument used to measure temperature is called a thermometer.

  • When the bulb of a thermometer touches a hot object, the mercury or alcohol present in its bulb expands and rises in the glass tube.
  • When the bulb touches a cold object, the mercury or alcohol contracts and falls in the tube.
  • If we bring a thermometer near a lighted bulb, the temperature will rise, because a lighted bulb gives out heat as well as light.

Direction of Heat Flow

Heat always flows from a hotter thing to a colder thing. If you hold a glass of cold water (05 degrees C) in a room (30 degrees C), heat flows from your hand (37 degrees C) into the cold water, and heat also flows from the room air (30 degrees C) into the cold water. Both flows of heat point into the glass of water.

lessons.title: Electrical Energy and Its Transformations
lessons.notes_html:
Energy Transformations

Electrical energy can be transformed into other forms of energy:

  • A heater changes electrical energy into heat.
  • A bulb changes electrical energy into light.
  • A loudspeaker changes electrical energy into sound.
  • In a television set, electrical energy is transformed into light energy (the picture) and sound energy.

Note: heat, light and sound are all correct transformations of electrical energy according to the lesson. Only plastic is not a form of energy.

Completing an Electric Circuit

To make an electric circuit complete so that the bulb lights up, the nail and the key should be connected at the ends of the wire. Both are made of metal, and metals are conductors of electricity. The cotton bud, plastic ball pen and ice-cream stick are insulators and will not complete the circuit.

The Reflector in a Torch

A torch with a reflector shines more light on a wall than a torch without one. The reflector gathers the light from the bulb and sends it forward in one direction, so more light reaches the wall.

Project Activity: Let Us Make a Telephone

Make holes in two paper cups and join them with a string or thin wire about seven metres long. Pull the string tight, and speak into one cup while a friend listens at the other. Sound vibrations travel along the tight string.

lessons.title: Force: Push and Pull
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Force?

A force is a push and pull. We apply force when we push a door, pull a drawer, or press play dough to change its shape.

How Force and Motion Are Related

Force and motion are closely related: applying a force can start motion in a body at rest, stop a moving body, change its speed, or change its direction. Without a force, a body does not change its state of motion.

lessons.title: Motion
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Motion?

A process in which an object changes its position is called motion. When a body changes its position, it is in motion.

Types of Movement around Us

  • A seesaw moves up and down.
  • A merry-go-round moves in a circle.
  • A swing moves back and forth.

A seesaw is in a state of rest until children sit and apply force on it; as a result, the seesaw moves up and down.

lessons.title: Gravity
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Gravity?

Gravity is the force with which the Earth pulls everything towards itself. All bodies are attracted towards the Earth due to gravity.

On Which Objects Does Gravity Act?

Gravity acts on all objects, whether they are near the Earth or far from it. It is gravity that brings falling leaves and dropped things down to the ground.

lessons.title: Friction
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Friction?

Friction is the force that opposes motion when two surfaces rub against each other. It always acts in the opposite direction to the motion. It is the force that stops, or tends to stop, moving objects: when you kick a football, it stops after covering a certain distance because of friction.

Advantages of Friction

Friction plays a very important role in our daily lives. Igniting a match stick, driving a nail into wood or a wall, and slowing and stopping vehicles by brakes are all possible due to friction. We cannot walk on Earth without friction.

Friction and Surfaces

  • If we apply the same force on a toy car, it will travel longer on a marble floor than on rocky soil, a floor of bricks or the ground, because the marble floor is smooth and has less friction.
  • We cannot walk on ice easily because ice is very smooth, so there is very little friction between our shoes and the ice, and our feet slip.

Choosing the Right Shoes

  • The strong, hard-soled shoe with a deep tread is suitable for a rocky surface, because its grip protects the feet and stops slipping on rough stones.
  • The light, comfortable sports shoe is for the playground, because it is soft and easy to run and play in.
  • The shoe with a rough or spiked sole is for an icy surface, because it increases friction and stops the feet from slipping on ice.

Friction in Writing

While writing, we use a push force — we push the pencil forward across the paper to form the letters. Friction between the pencil tip and the paper rubs off tiny particles of graphite that leave the mark on the paper, and friction also gives the grip that lets us control the pencil.

lessons.title: Simple Machines
lessons.notes_html:
What Is a Machine?

A machine is a device that makes our work easier. It works for us by changing the size or the direction of the force we apply, so we can lift heavy loads or do work with less effort.

Some Simple Machines

  • Pulley — the machine that consists of a grooved wheel. It is used for hoisting a flag.
  • Lever — a simple machine used to lift heavy objects.
  • Inclined plane — a sloping surface (a ramp) that lets us move things up with less force.
  • Gear — a toothed wheel machine.

The Inclined Plane Helps the Patient

An inclined plane (a ramp) is useful to take a patient sitting in a wheelchair onto a stage. A ramp lets the wheelchair be pushed up gradually with much less force than lifting it straight up.

Project Activity: Making a Pulley for Hoisting a Flag

Make a flagpole in the school playground with a bamboo pole, an iron hanger, a small wooden reel, a rope, the flag of Pakistan, a plumb line and some bricks, then hoist the national flag with this pulley.

lessons.title: Natural Resources
lessons.notes_html:
The Earth and Its Resources

Almost everything we use is made from natural resources. Even things made in factories come from materials taken from nature, such as metals from rocks, wood from trees, and plastic from oil. There is nothing that is not made from natural resources.

Land and Water on Earth

About 29 percent of the Earth's surface is land. The rest is covered with water.

Minerals

The solid non-living chemicals present in the Earth are called minerals.

Glass Is Made from Sand

Glass is made from sand. Sand, soil and other materials of the Earth are used to make many things of daily life.

lessons.title: Water on Earth
lessons.notes_html:
How Water Reaches Oceans and Lakes

Water reaches oceans and lakes through rivers and streams that flow downhill into them, and also directly through rain and the melting of snow and glaciers.

Why Is Water Not Available to Everyone?

Water is a renewable resource, but it is not equally available everywhere: much of it is salty sea water, many places get little rain, and water is wasted and polluted, so many people do not get enough clean drinking water.

Project Activity

Make a model of the flow of water from a glacier to the sea using suitable materials, showing how melting ice feeds rivers that carry water to the sea.

lessons.title: Fossils
lessons.notes_html:
What Are Fossils?

Fossils are the remains or imprints of dead plants and animals preserved in rocks. They provide information about the organisms that lived on the Earth millions of years ago, including organisms that are now extinct.

Knowing an Animal's Feed from Its Skull

We know about the feed of animals whose skulls are found during an excavation from the shape of their teeth. Sharp canines show the animal ate meat, while large flat molars and incisors show the animal ate plants.

Can a Jellyfish Become a Fossil?

No, we normally cannot obtain a fossil of a jellyfish. Its body is soft and has no bones or shell, so it decays completely after death instead of being preserved in rocks.

lessons.title: Renewable and Non-Renewable Resources
lessons.notes_html:
Renewable Resources

Renewable resources can be replaced naturally in a short time, such as forests, water and solar energy.

Why Forests Are Renewable

Forests are called renewable resources because trees can be grown again. If trees are cut down and new trees are planted, the forest can be replaced in a reasonable time.

Non-Renewable Resources

Non-renewable resources take millions of years to form and cannot be replaced once used up, such as coal, oil and natural gas. Oil is an example of a non-renewable resource.

Using Resources Carefully

We cannot have more resources than those of the past. Non-renewable resources are being used up and cannot be replaced, so we must use all resources carefully and save them.

lessons.title: Deforestation and Conservation of Resources
lessons.notes_html:
Deforestation: Advantages and Disadvantages

  • Advantages: land becomes available for farming and houses, and wood is obtained for fuel and furniture.
  • Disadvantages: animals lose their homes, and the soil is washed away and rainfall decreases.

Recycling

To make things reusable is called recycling. Recycling is a part of the conservation of resources: we should save water, plant more trees and use resources wisely so that they remain available for the future.

lessons.title: Weather and Climate
lessons.notes_html:
Weather

Weather is the daily condition of the environment or atmosphere of a location. It may continue the same for many days, or it may change suddenly. Weather is described in terms of temperature, humidity in the air, precipitation (rain or snow), clouds and winds of that particular location. Various factors including sunlight, air pressure, wind speed and clouds play important roles in the change of weather.

Climate

Climate is the general and long-lasting weather condition of a region on Earth — the general weather condition of a region over a long period of time.

Meteorology

Meteorology is the study of weather conditions. The experts who work in this field are called meteorologists. They provide us information about conditions like rain, wind, storm or heatwave in advance.

Note: unlike the other chapters, this chapter's exercises in the book are short answers, Constructed Response Questions, Investigate and Project only — there is no multiple-choice section.

lessons.title: Weather Instruments
lessons.notes_html:
Instruments Used to Study Weather

Weather conditions are analysed by using the following instruments:

InstrumentWhat It Measures
ThermometerThe temperature of air
BarometerThe pressure of air
AnemometerThe speed and direction of wind
Rain gaugeThe amount of rain

The movement of winds and clouds in the upper atmosphere of a region helps us predict the change in weather conditions for the next few days.

Project Activities

  • Construct a simple wind vane using cardboard or an old carton, scissors, a straw, board pins and coloured chart paper, as shown in the pictures in the book.
  • Make a simple rain gauge from a transparent plastic bottle, scissors, adhesive tape and a paper strip marked in millimetre scale, and use it to compare the amount of rain that fell in three days during a rainy season.

lessons.title: Why Climate Changes from Place to Place
lessons.notes_html:
Climate and Height from Sea Level

The higher a place is above sea level, the colder its climate becomes. That is why mountain areas are colder than places near the sea coast.

Climate and Distance from the Equator

Places near the Equator receive direct rays of the Sun and stay hot, while places far from the Equator receive slanting rays spread over a larger area, so they are colder.

Skardu and Karachi

In winter, the temperature of Skardu, a city of Gilgit-Baltistan, is below zero degree centigrade, while the temperature of Karachi is mild. Skardu is a high mountain city far from the sea, so its winter temperature falls below zero. Karachi is at sea level near the coast, and the sea keeps its temperature mild even in winter.

lessons.title: Climate Zones of the Earth
lessons.notes_html:
Three Climate Zones

On the basis of climate, the Earth is divided into three kinds of zones:

  • Torrid (Tropical) Zone — around the Equator.
  • Temperate Zones — North and South, in the middle.
  • Frigid (Polar) Zones — around the North and South Poles.

Climate of the Zones and Its Reasons

  • The Torrid Zone is hot all year because the Sun shines directly overhead.
  • The Temperate Zones are moderate because the Sun's rays fall slantingly.
  • The Frigid Zones are extremely cold because the rays fall very slantingly and ice reflects most of the heat. In the Polar Zone, much of the heat is reflected back by ice and snow, so very little warmth remains.

Pakistan's Zone

Based on climate, Pakistan is located in the North Temperate Zone, which has a moderate climate with hot summers and cool winters, while its northern mountains are cold.

lessons.title: Weather on the Moon and Changing Climate
lessons.notes_html:
Global Change in Climate

The last section of this chapter is about the global change in climate and the effect of human activities on the Earth.

Investigate: Weather on the Moon

There are no weather conditions on the Moon, because the Moon has almost no atmosphere. So there are no storms, rains or snowfall on the Moon. Its climate is extremely harsh — very hot in sunlight and extremely cold in darkness.

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Solar System and Our Earth

lessons.title: The Solar System and the Sun
lessons.notes_html:
The Solar System

The Sun is a huge sphere of burning gases. The gravity of the Sun keeps the planets and other celestial bodies together in the Solar System. The Solar System also has five dwarf planets.

Planets and the Sun

  • Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun.
  • Venus is the planet of the Solar System that does not have any moon (as given in the book's exercise).
  • Jupiter and Saturn have many moons.

Investigate: If the Sun Stopped Giving Light and Heat

If the Sun stopped providing light and heat, the Earth would become dark and extremely cold, plants would die because they could not make food, and animals and humans would soon die too. Life would not be possible on the Earth without the Sun.

lessons.title: The Moon
lessons.notes_html:
The Moon

The Moon revolves around the Earth. It completes its one revolution around the Earth in about 27 days. The Moon has no atmosphere.

Why Do We See Only One Side of the Moon?

We can only see one side of the Moon because the Moon takes the same time to spin on its own axis as it takes to revolve around the Earth, so the same side always faces the Earth.

lessons.title: Rotation of the Earth: Day and Night
lessons.notes_html:
Two Movements of the Earth

  • The Earth's spin on its own axis is its axial movement (rotation).
  • The Earth's movement around the Sun is its orbital movement (revolution).

Likewise, the Moon's spin on its axis is axial movement, and its movement around the Earth is orbital movement.

Day and Night

The Earth rotates on its axis, so the part of the Earth facing the Sun has day and the part facing away has night. The changing shadows during the day are also caused by the axial rotation of the Earth.

Pakistan on the Globe

On the globe, Pakistan is situated in the Northern Hemisphere.

lessons.title: Revolution of the Earth: Seasons
lessons.notes_html:
One Revolution around the Sun

The Earth completes its one revolution around the Sun in 365 days. This period is called a solar year.

Note: in the book's exercise, the word "rotation" is printed where revolution (movement around the Sun) is meant.

Why Seasons Change

Seasons change due to the annual revolution of the Earth and the tilt of its axis.

  • If there were no tilt in the Earth's axis, there would be no change of seasons. Every place would have the same weather all year round.
  • When it is winter in the Northern Hemisphere, it is summer in the Southern Hemisphere, because the two hemispheres receive the Sun's rays oppositely.

Seasons in the Southern Hemisphere

  • 21 March — autumn
  • 22 June — winter
  • 23 September — spring
  • 22 December — summer

These are the opposite of the seasons in the Northern Hemisphere on the same dates.

lessons.title: Solar and Lunar Eclipses
lessons.notes_html:
Solar Eclipse

In a solar eclipse, the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth, and the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth.

Lunar Eclipse

In a lunar eclipse, the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, and the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

Why Is the Solar Eclipse Usually Partial?

A solar eclipse is usually partial because the Moon's dark shadow is very small and rarely falls fully on one place, and the alignment of the Sun, Moon and Earth is seldom perfect, so most places see only a part of the Sun covered.

Project Activity

Make two groups in the class. One group will make the model of a lunar eclipse and the other group will make the model of a solar eclipse.

lessons.title: Working with Paper: Folding, Cutting and Pasting
lessons.notes_html:
Basic Craft Making

In this chapter we learn folding, cutting, tearing and pasting paper and cardboard to make useful objects, such as a paper bag and a greeting card.

Why a Line Is Drawn before Cutting

A line is drawn on the paper before cutting so that the scissors follow the line and the paper is cut straight and exactly to the required size and shape.

Making an Envelope from Square Paper

Yes, an envelope can be made from a square-shaped paper. By folding the four corners of the square towards the centre and pasting three of them, a pocket is formed that works as an envelope.

lessons.title: Making Models with Clay
lessons.notes_html:
Preparation of Clay

Models are made from a soft, sticky material. The book shows the preparation of clay for making models.

Why Any Soil Cannot Be Used

Any soil cannot be used to make a model because ordinary soil is loose and crumbly and does not hold its shape. A model needs a soft, sticky material like clay or playdough that keeps the shape given to it.

lessons.title: Mobile Phones
lessons.notes_html:
Using a Mobile Phone

  • Taking photographs of oneself is known as a selfie.
  • A photograph of a person is called a portrait.

Investigate: Mobile Phones of the Future

Mobile phone technology is progressing rapidly because people want faster communication, internet, cameras and many uses in one small device, and better chips and networks keep being developed. The mobile phone of the future will be even smarter, thinner and faster, with foldable screens and many more uses in daily life.

lessons.title: Shapes in Everyday Life
lessons.notes_html:
Cone and Prism

A cone has one circular base and one pointed top, while a prism has two identical flat ends (for example two triangles) joined by rectangular faces. A cone has a curved surface, while a prism has only flat surfaces.

Corners, Edges and Surfaces

Cube8126
Triangular pyramid464
Cone112
Triangular prism695

So a prism (triangular prism) has 6 corners, and a cube has 6 surfaces.

Examples of Shapes around Us

  • Circle: a coin and a plate.
  • Cube: a dice and a box.
  • Cylinder: a glass and a tin.
  • Cone: an ice-cream cone and a funnel.
  • Prism: a tent and a Toblerone chocolate box.

Cutting a Circle into Equal Parts

  • A circle cut into 2 equal parts: each part is 1/2 of the total.
  • A circle cut into 3 equal parts: each part is 1/3.
  • A circle cut into 4 equal parts: each part is 1/4.
  • A circle cut into 5 equal parts: each part is 1/5.
  • A circle cut into 6 equal parts: each part is 1/6.

lessons.title: First Aid and Measuring Health
lessons.notes_html:
The First Aid Box

A first aid box contains items used for immediate help, such as bandage, spirit, medical tape and tweezers. An instant cold pack is used to reduce inflammation as a first aid.

Clinical Thermometer

  • A clinical thermometer is used to check fever.
  • A clinical thermometer is shaken a few times before use so that the mercury thread falls back below 35 degrees C. This resets the thermometer, so it can correctly measure the patient's body temperature.

Blood Pressure

The blood pressure 160/100 is high blood pressure. The book also shows how to use a digital blood pressure monitor.

Project Activity: Making a Nest

Take an empty pack of juice or milk. Cut a face large enough for a small bird to enter and exit easily, pad the interior with cotton or cloth, drill a hole and insert a wire through the upper edge, and cover the pack with colour ribbons and packing paper. Then hang the nest near your home or school and observe whether any bird uses it.
